en: Bruno Miragem is particularly important at this point, because he makes quite clear that the CDC operates on the basis of functional and relational categories, and not of rigid ontological compartments. The author observes that the Brazilian legislator did not directly define the “consumer relationship”, preferring to conceptualize its subjects — consumer and supplier — and its object — product or service. For that very reason, these are relational and dependent concepts: there will only be a consumer if there is also a supplier, as well as a product or service, so that these definitions do not stand in isolation, and must appear jointly to trigger the application of the Code <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 139])</2>. The application of the CDC does not depend on excessively formalistic or classificatory fits, but on the concrete verification of a relational dynamic in which a vulnerable final recipient becomes bound to a market agent around a supplied utility. This same reading appears when Miragem states that the scope of the consumer law microsystem was defined precisely on the basis of the notion of the subjects of the consumer relationship and of its object, these being, once again, relational concepts, that is, legal positions that only reveal themselves within a concrete relationship <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 31])</4>. The point is especially useful because it shows that consumer, supplier, product and service are not watertight categories, designed to artificially limit the CDC's field of application, but keys of functional reading capable of capturing the economic reality actually at hand. It is precisely this key that matters to the present item. In complex digital supplies, the central question should not be whether the object fits comfortably into old civil-law taxonomies, but whether there is, in practice, a final recipient, a market professional and a utility offered in a context of vulnerability. Miragem thus helps to show that the CDC already has sufficient language to reach sophisticated techno-digital relationships, provided that its categories are read functionally. The gain is great: less classificatory fetish, more fidelity to the way the consumer relationship really happens. <5>↩</5>

Vulnerability is not a lateral element of the consumer relationship, but a structuring presupposition of the very protective application of the CDC. The system does not protect the consumer despite their fragility; it protects them precisely because it recognizes that fragility as a constitutive datum of the consumer market. The Manual recovers Antonio Herman Benjamin's formulation according to which vulnerability is the “fundamental piece” and the “starting point” of the entire application of consumer law, especially in contractual matters, which is why, in light of arts. 2 and 4, I, a true presumption of vulnerability operates in favor of natural persons who are final recipients of products and services <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 168])</2>. The STJ case law cited by the work goes in the same direction when it states that the starting point of the CDC is the principle of the consumer's vulnerability, understood as a mechanism intended to guarantee formal-material equality between the subjects of the consumer relationship and to illuminate the application of the protective and rebalancing norms in pursuit of equitable justice <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 118])</4>. Thus, the legal consumer relationship is not defined merely by the abstract presence of persons at its poles, but by the presence of a vulnerable party and of a supplier, which may justify the application of the CDC even in relationships between legal entities <5>Bessa</5><6>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 166])</6>. <7>↩</7>

The consumer's vulnerability, in Rizzatto Nunes, does not appear as a lateral or occasional element of the consumer relationship, but as a structural presupposition of the very protective application of the CDC. The decisive point lies not only in possible economic inferiority, but in the technical asymmetry that separates consumer and supplier within the productive process. The consumer enters the market without taking part in the definition, elaboration or control of the goods and services offered to them, which is why they occupy a position of objective fragility before productive models unilaterally organized by the supplier. As the author states, the consumer is “the weak element” of this market formation, precisely because they are “admittedly vulnerable as a recipient of the production models unilaterally defined and imposed by the supplier”, being moreover a “mere spectator at the spectacle of production” <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 72])</2>. This finding deepens when vulnerability is also read in its informational dimension. Nunes stresses that the consumer not only stands outside the productive system, but also lacks the technical conditions needed to understand its functioning or to assess, on equal terms, the products and services presented to them. The consumer's fragility thus stems from the lack of command over the processes, criteria and information that structure the offer, which justifies the corrective intervention of consumer law as an instrument for the material realization of equality. Along these lines, the author notes that the law recognizes the fact that the consumer “not only has no access to the productive system but has no means of knowing how it works”, which is why they must be understood as “the weak party of the legal consumer relationship” <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 457])</4>. <5>↩</5>

Rizzatto Nunes's reading is particularly useful at this point because it puts the classificatory problem back in its proper scale: the core of art. 3 of the CDC lies not in restricting the reach of protection to corporeal objects or simple performances, but in ensuring that consumer-law protection applies to every supply relationship economically organized for the market. On this view, the legal concept of product was deliberately formulated in comprehensive terms, precisely to prevent escape zones from the protective regime, also reaching immaterial goods and incorporeal utilities made available to the consumer. As the author summarizes, the law adopted concepts “as generic as possible” because “the aim is that nothing escapes it”, so that even performances traditionally perceived as intangible can already be framed as immaterial goods for purposes of the CDC's application <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 97])</2>. The same logic projects onto the concept of service. Nunes observes that not every consumer performance presents itself in a linear or isolated form, there being simple services, composite services and structures in which the final utility depends on the articulation between multiple agents, instrumental activities and even aggregated products. For that reason, supply is not exhausted in the one-off act of delivery, also encompassing the maintenance of the functional architecture necessary for the enjoyment of the contracted utility. In the author's words, there are services “composed of others” and also cases in which the performance is organized “through the use of products” <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 198])</4>. This framing is especially relevant for immaterial supplies in a digital environment, in which the consumer experience depends less on an isolated thing and more on the operational continuity of a technical, communicational and relational infrastructure set in motion by the supplier. <5>↩</5>

Commenting on paragraph 2 of art. 3, Filomeno recalls that service is “any activity supplied in the consumer market, for remuneration”, observing that the Code covers “each and every type of service”, understood as a utility enjoyed by the consumer and provided by a given supplier, in a facere <1>Filomeno</1><2>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 110])</2>. The formulation is especially useful because it takes the legal concept back to its simplest material matrix: service, in the consumer-law regime, is the provision of utility in the form of a doing, without this authorizing narrow readings or formalistic classifications aimed at withdrawing protection. This basis is reinforced when Filomeno recalls that, in the genesis of the Code, the terms “goods and services” were chosen as unequivocal and generic expressions precisely to point the applier to the real objects of interest of consumer relationships, while at the same time excluding, by contrast, relationships of another nature, such as tax relationships <3>Filomeno</3><4>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 110])</4>. The value of his observation lies in showing that the CDC is born committed to a material reading of the consumer relationship, centered on the economic utility concretely supplied to the final recipient. Before any later sophistication about the product–service dichotomy, the system's starting point is already settled on broad, functional categories oriented toward consumer protection, and not on conceptual barriers designed to narrow it. <5>↩</5>

Filomeno treat the consumer's vulnerability as a structural presupposition of consumer-law protection. The author observes that, for evident reasons, among them the consumer's absolute lack of control over the products and services placed on the market and the absolute disproportion between their bargaining power and that of suppliers, one starts from the presupposition that the consumer is the vulnerable party in the consumer relationship, which justifies unequal legal treatment between naturally unequal parties and direct protective governmental action <1>Filomeno</1><2>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 61])</2>. The application of the CDC is not explained by classificatory formalism, but by a material finding of structural fragility that calls for normative correction. This vulnerability, moreover, is not reduced to possible economic insufficiency. Filomeno describes it as the consumer's fragility before the supplier also in informational and technical aspects, that is, with regard both to purchasing power and to the information made available and the specialized knowledge held by the supplier itself <3>Filomeno</3><4>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 61])</4>. For that very reason, the recognition of this vulnerability has a direct impact on contractual dogmatics: as the author notes, the finding that the consumer is the vulnerable party in consumer relationships causes the classical dogmas of full autonomy of the will, abstract equality and contractual intangibility to yield, precisely because such principles would only hold in full if the parties had equal real power of decision <5>Filomeno</5><6>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 346])</6>. Consumer-law protection is already born, in its classical basis, founded on vulnerability as a structural datum of the relationship and not as an episodic exception. <7>↩</7>

The interpretation of the consumer contractual relationship, especially in contexts of complex, continuous or technically governed supply, must start less from abstract formal framings and more from the consumer's material vulnerability and from the way the supply is actually organized and operates. This means that the application of the CDC cannot be held hostage to superficial classificatory appearances, nor to an idealized image of parity between the parties, when the reality of the bond reveals mass contracting, unilateral pre-drafting of terms, organizational opacity and the adhering party's practical dependence on the supplier's structure. Marques makes this point explicit when she observes that adhesion contracts and general contract conditions work as a strong indication of factual vulnerability, even when the contracting party, in theory, has technical training or a professional activity. In the author's words, “most banking contracts are concluded through the use of general contract conditions and adhesion contracts. These methods of mass contracting […] serve as an indication of the co-contracting party's vulnerability. Even if the co-contracting party is a lawyer, even if a merchant or farmer, factual vulnerability will almost always be present” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 613)</2>. This insight becomes even more relevant when the supply does not end in a one-off act but extends over time as an organized, repeated relationship functionally closed around the consumer. In these cases, vulnerability is not a mere episodic accident of the contractual moment, but a structural condition of the user's insertion into a regime of dependent enjoyment. Marques describes this logic when discussing services provided through organized networks, whose internal functioning often escapes the consumer's awareness and which, in the contemporary context, tend to bind the consumer ever more captively to the supplier or chain of suppliers. As the author notes, these are services that “bind the consumer in such a way that, over the years of the complex contractual relationship, they become a ‘captive’ client of that supplier or chain of suppliers, becoming dependent even on the maintenance of that contractual relationship or seeing all their expectations frustrated.” <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 109)</4> Applied to the present problem, this reading reinforces that the legal qualification of the bond must take into account the real form of the supply and the vulnerability it concretely produces, and not merely formal labels that, used. <5>↩</5>

Factual vulnerability is a structural presupposition of consumer-law protection. Miragem observes that consumer law belongs among the so-called protective rights, whose raison d'être necessarily rests on a situation of factual inequality, which they seek to redress by means of the protective norm <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 34])</2>. The application of the CDC is thus explained not by a formal abstraction of categories, but by the material finding that the consumer relationship is marked by a real asymmetry between its parties, which calls for normative intervention aimed at restoring balance. The principle of vulnerability is the basic principle that grounds the existence and application of consumer law. The very existence of consumer law is justified by the recognition of the consumer's vulnerability in the consumer market, and it is precisely this vulnerability that requires the law to concern itself with the consumer's protection <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 122])</4>. The point is central because it shows that vulnerability is not an accidental, peripheral or complementary element of the microsystem, but its cornerstone. When product, service and complex digital supplies are at issue, the center of the analysis should not be a somewhat bureaucratic cult of classification for its own sake, but the protective function of the CDC in the face of a structurally unequal relationship. Miragem thus helps to recall an important obvious point: consumer, supplier, product and service make dogmatic sense only within a system built to respond to vulnerability. And it is precisely for this reason that these categories must be read in a functional and broad way, faithful to market reality, not a narrow or ornamental one. <5>↩</5>

Bruno Torquato Zampier Lacerda's doctrine of digital assets<1><2>630</2></1> performs an important function because it resolves, with considerable depth, a problem that cannot be sidestepped by contractual rhetoric or by nostalgia for tangibility: techno-digital assets are legal goods and do not vanish from the world of Law merely because they are incorporeal. Digitally organized information can acquire a utility of its own, become part of the subject's sphere of interests and, for that reason, be treated as a legally relevant incorporeal good, with or without immediate economic content <3>Lacerda</3><4>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 51; p. 57; p. 72)</4><5><6>631</6></5>. This starting point is correct and indispensable. Without it, the debate on continuous digital consumption would be held hostage to the crude fiction that everything that cannot be held in the hand is legally light, dissolvable and disposable at the supplier's mere will.

Another real gain of this framework is the recognition that, once admitted as goods, these assets become susceptible to appropriation, circulation, enjoyment and protection. They enter the legal world not as conceptual curiosities, but as objects capable of sustaining organized legal positions, including use, enjoyment, disposal and transfer. Incorporeality neither prevents the exercise of the faculties typical of ownership nor turns enjoyment into a gracious tolerance granted by technology <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 73; p. 82; p. 151)</2><3><4>632</4></3>. This matters a great deal here <5>p. 566</5> because it rules out, from the outset, the semantic fraud of the “revocable license” as a formula capable of making everything already economically incorporated into the user's sphere evaporate. If there is an identifiable virtual object, associated with the account and enjoyed within the ecosystem, there is legal substance to be taken seriously, even if the platform tries to cloak it in a vocabulary of precariousness.

Riot's own contractual clauses help to show this. The company expressly defines “Virtual Content” as a set that includes in-game currency, champions, skins, emotes, accessories and other items associated with the account<1><2>633</2></1>, and admits that this content may be obtained not only by conventional purchase, but also by earning, reward, gift or other internal dynamics of the ecosystem<3><4>634</4></3>. This is useful for two reasons. First, because it shows that the contractual design itself recognizes an identifiable core of enjoyment associated with the account, which dismantles the puerile thesis that the object does not legally exist. Second, because it shows that the formation of this core does not end in a one-off market exchange, but takes place within a continuing dynamic of progression, circulation, reward and participation. There, the consumed object is born less as an isolated “digital thing” and more as a position of enjoyment produced and maintained within a governed environment.

The concept of the digital asset also renders another useful service by providing an internal typology of the phenomenon. Not every techno-digital asset has the same structure, function or regime, and the distinction between patrimonial, existential and mixed assets helps keep everything from being treated as an amorphous mass. This classification makes it possible to allocate the effects of ownership, use, transfer and protection more accurately, and it shows that certain digital assets gravitate closer to the patrimonial sphere, others closer to personality, and many combine both <1>p. 567</1> dimensions <2>Lacerda</2><3>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 56; p. XIV; p. 146)</3><4><5>635</5></4>. Such refinement is useful and should not be discarded. The problem is that it still organizes the phenomenon mainly around the asset, whereas the core of the IOC demands a reading oriented by governed enjoyment.

It is here that the thesis turns. The gain of the civil-law doctrine lies in resolving the problem of the legal status of the techno-digital asset and in blocking the nominalist dissolution of what has already entered the user's sphere. But when the conflict shifts to platform consumption involving continuing, mutable enjoyment dependent on private governance, the civil-law axis of ownership does not by itself capture the heart of the problem. The IOC regime starts from the same recognition of legal status, but shifts the focus: instead of asking predominantly who “has” the asset and how it circulates or is transferred, it asks how enjoyment is maintained, modulated, degraded, made intelligible and restorable over time. It is a change of axis, not a denial of the previous step.

It is worth being explicit about the nature of this change of axis, because it is often read, without due attention, as a simple move from one library shelf to another. The project of the doctrine of digital assets is dogmatically delimited and responds to a recognizable problem. It operates within civil law and confronts, first and foremost, the silence of the Brazilian legal order about an entire class of assets that exists, circulates and produces economic and affective effects, but had no express regime of existence, ownership, transfer and extinction. Lacerda fills this silence with functional taxonomy and classificatory rigor, and that is why the work has become a canonical reference for digital inheritance, for the succession of digital assets and for the civil-law protection of the subject's digital estate. The service rendered is real and cannot be treated as a mere disposable preparatory stage. <1>p. 568</1> When this framework is called upon to answer what it set out to answer, it answers well.

The present thesis, however, operates in a different domain and responds to a different problem. It confronts not the silence of the Civil Code on the status of the digital asset, but the opacity of the Consumer Protection Code on the regime of the immaterial product under continuing and governed enjoyment. This shift of domain is not a detail of disciplinary organization. It carries a structuring dogmatic consequence, because civil law regulates relationships between formally equal subjects, while consumer law regulates structurally asymmetric relationships under mandatory public policy. Where the civil-law doctrine asks to whom the good belongs, how it circulates and how it is extinguished, the IOC regime asks how the promised utility is maintained, modulated, degraded and restorable over time. The questions are not opposed. They inhabit distinct layers of the phenomenon and call for correspondingly distinct techniques of attribution.

The difference between these layers can be described more sharply through a temporal distinction. The doctrine of digital assets works with a predominantly static ontology of the asset. The good exists, is classifiable, can have an owner, can be transferred, can be extinguished. There is, so to speak, a photograph of the asset, and the relevant legal faculties are organized around that photograph. The IOC regime, in turn, works with a processual ontology of enjoyment. The immaterial object of consumption cannot be captured in a static photograph because its identity lies not in a synchronic cross-section, but in a diachronic course of maintenance, updating, curation and administration. It is, in a legally relevant sense, what is continuously made of it within the environment that produces it. That is why the passage from the civil-law grammar to the consumer-law grammar is not merely a change of applicable code. It is the recognition that the time of performance is part of the very existence of the consumed object.

This temporal difference explains, in part, why the axis of the conflict also shifts. In the typical scenarios addressed by the doctrine of digital assets, the controversy revolves around ownership, circulation and extinction. The questions are who the owner is, whether the good can be inherited, whether the platform can block it after death, whether contractual clauses can bar disposal <1>inter vivos</1> or <2>causa mortis</2>. These are relevant conflicts, and the civil-law framework is well equipped to address them. In the typical scenarios addressed by the IOC regime, however, the controversy revolves around enjoyment, modulation and functional integrity. The questions are whether the object is still what it promised to be, whether the unilateral alteration preserved sufficient functional equivalence, whether the degradation produced by an ordinary update exceeded a legally tolerable margin, whether the opacity of the environment allows the <3>p. 569</3> consumer to reconstruct institutionally what was altered. These are questions that the civil-law framework can formulate but has no natural tool to answer, because its instruments were forged for another type of litigation.

It is also worth situating the difference between the relevant subjects in the two constructions. For the doctrine of digital assets, the legally central subject is the owner of the digital asset, often the user as holder of a digital estate whose preservation, transfer or allocation is in dispute. The vulnerability that matters in this framework is, as a rule, the existential vulnerability linked to the owner's personality or the patrimonial vulnerability linked to their holdings. For the IOC regime, the legally central subject is the consumer under a platform, living, active and in a continuous relationship with a supplier that concentrates architecture, curation, enforcement and the production of meaning. The vulnerability that matters here is contemporary factual vulnerability, of which semiotic vulnerability is a current specification, and it is not to be confused with any of the figures the civil-law framework has traditionally worked with. The two vulnerabilities coexist in digital environments, but call for different protection techniques and activate distinct normative sources.

It should also be noted, for the sake of methodological honesty, that these differences do not make the doctrine of digital assets irrelevant to the present work. On the contrary, they reveal how precisely that doctrine must be invoked. Lacerda blocks, with a force that could hardly be achieved by any other route, the semantic fraud that would dissolve the digital asset into a mere permission of use revocable at any time. This block is irreplaceable, because without it the platform would win the controversy by private dictionary before it was even framed as a legal controversy. The doctrine of digital assets builds, in other words, the floor from which the debate on regime becomes possible. If the asset is legally light, dissolvable by mere contractual nomenclature and disposable at the supplier's unilateral will, any discussion of continuing enjoyment, functional equivalence and auditability becomes idle talk about something whose legal existence has not even been stabilized. Lacerda stabilizes that existence. This is the point of departure of the present thesis.

The methodological relationship between the two constructions can then be summarized in terms that reject both artificial competition and simulated continuity. The doctrine of digital assets rigorously answers the question of whether the techno-digital asset is a good. The IOC regime answers, with its own instruments, the question of whether the immaterial object of consumption remains enjoyable, in legally equivalent terms, within platform ecosystems. One builds the legal status of the asset; the other builds the legal regime of its continuous governance. One resolves the entry of the digital object into the world of law; the other <1>p. 570</1> resolves the persistence of the promised utility within a consumer relationship whose performance does not end with the initial act. That is why the thesis, instead of simulating that it has surpassed the prior civil-law step, embraces it and repositions it in its proper function. Lacerda provides the premise of the asset's legal existence. The IOC provides the regime for supplying the enjoyment that this asset, now legally recognized, sustains over time.

This synthesis finally makes it possible to gauge clearly the dogmatic place that the doctrine of digital assets occupies in the edifice of this thesis. It is not a parallel track, nor a competing track, nor a prior track in a chronological sense that had to be surpassed. It is a contiguous and operationally complementary track, which addresses a layer of the phenomenon different from the one on which the present work concentrates and which, by virtue of that difference, makes the advance proposed here possible. Acknowledging this contiguity, instead of disguising it as competition, is an elementary requirement of dogmatic honesty.

Denying a contribution that structures the very possibility of the debate would, moreover, be rhetorically self-defeating, because it would weaken the floor from which the argument of governed enjoyment becomes intelligible. Recognizing the contribution in its proper measure, and marking precisely where the turn is necessary, is what allows the IOC regime to present itself as what it in fact is: an internal development of the consumer-law system based on the immaterial product already contained in art. 3, paragraph 1, of the Consumer Protection Code, built on a civil-law floor that seriously recognizes the legal existence of the digital asset and that, at the same time, leaves open the problem whose answer is the object of this thesis.

One further observation must be made before the comparison proceeds, because it concerns the way in which the doctrine of digital assets may be applied by third parties in concrete cases involving immaterial objects of consumption. The tripartite typology that distinguishes patrimonial, existential and mixed digital assets was formulated to answer problems of ownership, circulation and succession with precision, and it performs that role with recognized competence.

There is, however, a non-negligible operational risk when this same typology is invoked, without mediation, to resolve consumer disputes in platform environments. The risk is that the interpreter, faced with an object such as a skin, a champion, a cosmetic item, the ecosystem's internal currency or equivalent content associated with the account, immediately asks whether the asset is patrimonial, existential or mixed, and organizes the whole dispute around that classification as if it were enough to yield the applicable legal regime.

<1>p. 571</1> The question, even if technically well formulated on the civil-law plane, dispenses with the consumer-law microsystem before it is even invoked, because the taxonomy at play was forged to answer what the asset is considered in itself, and not what the governed enjoyment made of it within a continuing consumer relationship is. The practical effect of this elision is problematic. The case receives a civil-law framing that is coherent in its own logic, but loses the platform's governance layer, which is precisely where the dispute usually lies in cases of continuous digital consumption.

It is therefore worth recording the methodological position this thesis adopts. The patrimonial, existential and mixed taxonomy, considered in itself, is neither discarded nor demonized. It remains a useful instrument when the conflict actually turns on ownership, succession, post mortem allocation or inter vivos disposal of the digital asset, cases in which the civil-law floor offers a technically adequate answer. The point, however, is that applying this taxonomy to platform consumer disputes demands a prior methodological step, and that step is verifying that the object in question is not merely a digital asset considered generically, but an Immaterial Object of Consumption under governed enjoyment.

When this qualification holds, the relevant initial question is no longer about the patrimonial or existential nature of the asset but about the regime of the enjoyment that this asset sustains within the environment that produces it. This inversion of the order of questions does not annul the civil-law typology, but restores it to its proper function, preventing the classification of the asset from improperly absorbing the entire legal framing of the case and from neutralizing the public-policy protections that the consumer-law microsystem brings into play when the digital object appears as an object of consumption in an environment continuously governed by a supplier.

This shift matters because, on continuous consumption platforms, governance does not act from outside on an already complete digital good. It is part of the very legally relevant utility of the object. Maintenance, updating, curation, enforcement, parameterization and intelligibility of the environment are not incidental vicissitudes of a fully given thing; they are constitutive dimensions of enjoyment. That is why the IOC is formulated as a concretization of the CDC's immaterial product, and not as a simple static “digital thing” anchored in the Civil Code's book on goods<1><2>636</2></1>. The civil-law grammar serves to validate the <3>p. 572</3> legal existence of the asset; it is not enough to exhaust the consumer-law syntax of a form of consumption whose utility stabilizes only through continuous private administration.

This is the first relevant limit of the civil-law framework. It captures more sharply events of suppression, blocking, account termination, unavailability and transfer. It does an excellent job of showing that the digital object is not mist. The problem is that, in ecosystems of governed enjoyment, a decisive part of the conflict takes the form not of an abrupt withdrawal of the object, but of progressive functional erosion through ordinary modulation of the environment. The user apparently still has access to the object; yet its utility may be lowered by updates, balancing, reclassifications, interface changes, alterations of equivalence and continuous reorganizations of the regime of use. The nominal persistence of the asset, or even of the account, is not enough to rule out a defect. The conflict is no longer only about existence or availability, but about the substantial preservation of the function enjoyed.

The IOC category gains explanatory advantage by allowing continuing maintenance, modulation and administration to be treated as part of the consumer performance itself, and not as accidents external to an already formed good. This makes room for two <1>standards</1> that the purely civil-law framework sees less sharply: functional value equivalence, as a criterion for assessing a defect when utility is lowered without formal suppression, and open auditability, as a minimum requirement of controllability over relevant alterations in the supply regime. In other words, the IOC does not contest with the doctrine of digital assets the problem of “being a good”; it confronts the problem of “continuing to be enjoyable in a legally equivalent way”.

The second limit lies in the very idea of vulnerability. The civil-law framework tends to work well with technical disadvantage, classic informational asymmetry, ownership, access and availability. But in governed environments the consumer's vulnerability goes further. It is also semiotic. The perception of loss, of degradation and of how much a downgrade matters depends on signs, interfaces, metrics, rarities, narratives of prestige, showcases and framings controlled by the supplier itself.

The problem is not merely knowing less about the internal workings of the system, but depending on the platform's mediation to form expectations, measure value, perceive functional erosion and name what was actually lost. Where the platform controls not only the object but also the reference points by which the loss can be perceived and contested, vulnerability does not fit entirely within the classic schemes of informational deficit.

<1>p. 573</1> That is also why the critique of the rhetoric of the “revocable license” remains valuable, but not sufficient. The doctrine of digital assets is right to block the corporate attempt to requalify, by simple contractual nominalism, objects already integrated into the user's sphere as permissions dissolvable by unilateral will. When there is actual economic outlay or a relevant incorporation of utility into the subject's sphere, the language of the license is not enough to erase the legal density of the asset, nor to neutralize the application of public-policy norms <2>Lacerda</2><3>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 124; p. 193)</3><4><5>637</5></4>. This block is fundamental. Without it, the platform would always win by private dictionary. But even after this trick is barred, the central problem of the IOC remains: how to control, within an enjoyment that continues to exist, the ordinary mutations that corrode its functional and symbolic integrity?

The IOC regime recognizes that abusiveness does not necessarily reside entirely in a clause or in an event of overt blocking. In certain cases, it is built into the very design of the supply, when the architecture organizes inducement, extraction and the normalization of losses as an operating principle. The doctrine of digital assets is very helpful in identifying contractual nullities, arbitrary blocks and suppressions of assets. The IOC incorporates this layer, but adds another: reading architecture as conduct and abusive teleology as a design defect of the regime of governed enjoyment. This makes it possible to address not only abrupt withdrawal, but also managed deterioration.

That is why the function of this item is to provide a basis and a contrast, not a competing track. The doctrine of digital assets supports the crucial premise that digital assets are legal goods and that contractual precariousness is not the user's inevitable fate. At the same time, it reveals its own limits when the problem is no longer only ownership, transfer and availability, but the continuous governance of enjoyment. The IOC regime takes on the civil-law gain, rejects the straw man of the legal non-existence of the digital and repositions the debate on the ground <1>p. 574</1> that matters. It seeks the protection of using, the control of functional integrity and, in certain cases, the protection of being, whenever enjoyment incorporates the symbolic identity and biographical continuity of the consumer user.

The author is widely known as Bruno Zampier; however, the cataloging record of his work expressly gives Lacerda as his last surname, which is why, in this thesis, in compliance with the ABNT standard and the required formal conventions, the author is referred to by that surname and not by the better-known one. <1>↩</1>

The incorporeality of the techno-digital asset neither dissolves it into legal irrelevance nor authorizes treating it as a mere side effect of technology. In the information society, information itself comes to occupy the place of an object of legal relationships, either because it constitutes a directly appropriable interest or because its violation produces legally relevant injuries. In this light, the protection of information ceases to be a peripheral theme and becomes part of the very core of the legal protection of the person and of their interests in the digital environment <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 51)</2>. Digitally organized information can acquire a utility of its own and, for that reason, be treated as a legally relevant incorporeal good, with or without immediate economic content. Utility matters more here than tangibility: digital assets may correspond both to economically exploitable assets and to personal projections whose legal relevance derives from their place in the subject's sphere of interests <3>Lacerda</3><4>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 57)</4>. This opening makes it possible to recognize seriously that incorporeality does not prevent appropriation, enjoyment or protection. The civil-law framework of digital assets thus resolves an essential problem: that of the legal existence of the techno-digital asset. That is also why it is indispensable to this item. The critical point the thesis will introduce later lies not in denying this gain, which would be methodological foolishness, but in showing its limit. Recognizing the legal status of the asset and its place in the subject's sphere is still not enough, by itself, to resolve adequately the conflicts that arise when enjoyment is continuous, mutable and governed in platform ecosystems <5>Lacerda</5><6>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 72)</6>. <7>↩</7>

The legal status of digital assets does not end with their mere abstract existence. Once recognized as goods, they also become susceptible to appropriation, circulation, enjoyment and protection, that is, they enter the legal world not as conceptual curiosities, but as objects subject to legally organized faculties and powers. The doctrine of digital assets is right precisely in rejecting the idea that incorporeality would prevent use, enjoyment, disposal or transfer of the techno-digital asset <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 73)</2>. This consequence is decisive for the present item, because it dispels from the outset the fantasy that the digital asset would be legally light just because it cannot be held in the hand. If the owner can delete it, assign it, encumber it or transfer it, then we are already dealing with a good dense enough to support legal positions typical of ownership. The enjoyment of the digital asset is therefore not a mere gracious tolerance granted by technology; it can be legally organized and protected, including through the assignment of use to third parties as a corollary of the very exercise of the corresponding subjective right <3>Lacerda</3><4>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 82)</4>. This point is especially important because it strengthens the argument without resorting to terminological magic. The civil-law doctrine of digital assets forcefully resolves the problem of the asset's capacity to form part of an estate, to be enjoyed, to circulate in transactions and to receive legal protection. The insufficiency would lie not in this framework's inability to recognize the asset, but in the fact that, even while recognizing appropriation and circulation, it does not exhaust the conflicts of continuous enjoyment, unilateral mutability and functional governance in a platform environment <5>Lacerda</5><6>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 151)</6>. <7>↩</7>

“4.1. What is Virtual Content? (Virtual Content includes items such as in-game currency and virtual products, such as champions, skins, emotes, accessories etc). When using Riot's Services, we may offer you opportunities to acquire a limited license to access virtual goods, such as champions, skins, emotes etc., (“Virtual Products”) and in-game currency (“Game Currency”), associated with your account (together, referred to as “Virtual Content”). Game Currency may only be used for the specific game for which it was purchased, unless otherwise stated at the time of purchase.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. <3>↩</3>

“4.2. How do I get a “license” to access Virtual Content? (Buy, earn or receive.) We may offer you various opportunities to acquire a limited license to access Game Currency or Virtual Content, including: buying it (e.g., with a credit card); earning it (e.g., by completing missions or game tasks); or receiving it (e.g., from another player as a gift or by using the crafting functionality such as Hextech®).” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The usefulness of the doctrine of digital assets also lies in offering an internal criterion for organizing the phenomenon, which keeps all techno-digital reality from being treated as an amorphous mass. Not every digital asset has the same structure, function or regime. There are assets with clearly patrimonial content, assets of an existential character, and cases in which both dimensions appear in combination. This distinction matters because it allows the legal effects of ownership, use, transfer and protection to be allocated more precisely <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 56)</2>. This classificatory refinement is one of the most important gains of the civil-law framework, because it keeps the debate from getting stuck in vague generalities. Knowing whether the asset is patrimonial, existential or mixed is not academic taxonomic fussiness; it is what allows circulation, succession, the exercise of private autonomy and the protection of goods linked to the owner's personal sphere to be properly calibrated. The very adoption of this criterion in proposals for legislative reform shows that it is not a mere ornamental doctrinal invention, but a genuinely useful tool of legal work <3>Lacerda</3><4>(Lacerda, 2024, p. XIV)</4>. This gain must be honestly acknowledged because it strengthens, rather than weakens, the critical step of the thesis. The doctrine of digital assets classifies the asset well, distinguishes its species intelligently and provides a reliable compass for the rules on ownership and its circulation. The limit appears elsewhere: even with a good typology of the asset, the framework still does not fully resolve the problems that arise when the conflict no longer revolves only around ownership and comes to bear on continuous enjoyment, governed mutability and the functional integrity of the experience consumed on a platform <5>Lacerda</5><6>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 146)</6>. <7>↩</7>

Arts. 79 to 103 of the Civil Code provide the general classificatory background on goods, making it possible to situate technically the discussion of incorporeality, patrimoniality and the legal circulation of digital assets. Their function here is merely structural: to validate the use of the civil-law grammar of goods to recognize a minimum legal density in skins, virtual currencies and digital items, without shifting the dogmatic axis to pure civil law and without taking from the CDC the leading role in understanding and protecting the IOC. <1>↩</1>

The contractual language of the precarious or revocable license is not enough, by itself, to dissolve the legal density of a digital asset already incorporated into the user's sphere. When there is actual economic outlay to acquire digital content or utilities, the mere corporate requalification of the relationship as a “mere license” cannot operate as a semantic trick capable of disfiguring the existence of a digital estate. In other words, the fact that the platform calls it a license does not oblige Law to pretend that it never had patrimonial substance <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 124)</2>. The doctrine of digital assets makes it possible to state seriously that music libraries, video libraries, virtual libraries and other similar collections may form part of the user's estate, including for purposes of succession, despite corporate rhetoric to the contrary. The legal density of the good's incorporation into the subject's sphere does not disappear by private decree <3>Lacerda</3><4>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 124)</4>. The same logic extends to clauses that seek to neutralize access to, use of or disposal of these assets in terms incompatible with public-policy norms. Provisions that absolutely prohibit access to the asset or its legal allocation may be null when they collide with the general parameters of the system, including those prohibiting the advance waiver of rights in adhesion contracts <5>Lacerda</5><6>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 193)</6>. The value of this approach here is central: the doctrine of digital assets effectively blocks the nominalist dissolution of the asset. What the thesis will need to show later is that this block, although indispensable, still does not exhaust the problem when the enjoyment of the object is continuously governed, reconfigured and strained by the platform. <7>↩</7>

Art. 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC already offers a sufficient basis for understanding the IOC as an immaterial product. The law does not make the product conditional on corporeality, nor does it tie it to the image of a tangible thing delivered once and for all. By expressly admitting material and immaterial goods, the system is already open enough to encompass objects of consumption whose utility is organized in a digital environment and realized through continued enjoyment. Reading the IOC this way, therefore, does not project a foreign category onto the Code. It makes explicit a dogmatic possibility already contained in the legal text itself, and dispels the idea that digital consumption would always depend on precarious analogies with traditional material media (Nunes, 2018, [p. 96; p. 160]<1><2>638</2></1>; Nery Jr., 2011, p. 544-546<3><4>639</4></3>).

This legal openness matters because, in digital ecosystems, the object of consumption is not exhausted by abstract availability or by formally completed delivery. Its legal existence, as an object of consumption, depends on governed conditions of enjoyment. What the consumer acquires is not merely nominal access to an item or to an isolated utility, but a position of enjoyment whose functionality depends on maintenance, updating, modulation, intelligibility and continuity. The tradition of the CDC itself already allows this reading, because the <1>p. 575</1> core of the product category lies not in tangibility, but in utility economically organized to satisfy human needs <2>Filomeno</2><3>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 108-109; p. 111- 113])</3><4><5>640</5></4>. Consequently, the legal standing of the IOC does not arise from an exercise in fiction. It follows from the very normative structure of the immaterial product.

That is also why the contractual form of the license is not enough to dissolve the legal density of the acquired enjoyment. The Terms of Service of <1>Riot Games</1> expressly recognize a core of “Virtual Content” associated with the account, made up of in-game currency, <2>skins</2>, <3>emotes</3>, accessories and other items, and admit that this content may be formed through purchase, earning, gifting or other internal dynamics of the ecosystem. This shows that the supplier itself already works with an identifiable virtual object functionally integrated into the consumption environment. The IOC category starts from this fact, but puts it back on the right ground. What matters is not merely the existence of a virtual asset associated with the account, but the fact that its utility only stabilizes through the environment that makes it enjoyable. The clause helps prove the existence of the object. It does not exhaust its regime.

The proposed reconstruction, then, is functional. The CDC protects not only an isolated “object”, but also the conditions of enjoyment, access, maintenance and intelligibility that make it effectively consumable. In contemporary consumer relationships, what is offered to the consumer is a functional bundle of utilities, qualities, modes of performance, expectations and annexes that make up the very legal experience of the performance. The contractual object cannot remain tied to the image of the isolated material good, because protection already applies also to quality, functionality, information, status and security ensured in the relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 180; p. 183)</2><3><4>641</4></3>. It is exactly in this key that the IOC becomes <5>p. 576</5> intelligible. It legally names an object whose relevance lies not in a static existence, but in the enjoyment concretely organized and maintained over time.

This does not require a break with the grammar of the CDC. On the contrary, it stems from its evolutionary and functional use in the face of contemporary forms of supply. The system does not need to be replaced or remade. It needs to be read in close fit with the real problem it faces. The contemporary consumer also accumulates immaterial goods linked to leisure, security, information, status and well-being, and consumer law already has instruments to offer reasonable answers to these cases without abandoning its own protective matrix <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 70-71; p. 104)</2><3><4>642</4></3>. The IOC, thus, is not a heterodox graft. It is an internal development of the system itself, built on the immaterial product the law already provides for.

The doctrine of digital assets helps to confirm this starting point, because it blocks any relapse into a dogmatics dependent on physical tangibility. Information, provided it carries appreciable utility, may be treated as a legal good and as an immaterial good. This recognition is important for the thesis because it rules out denying the legal relevance of the techno-digital object and reinscribes its legal status on the plane of consumption <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 52; p. 55; p. 71)</2><3><4>643</4></3>. But the inflection of the IOC begins precisely where the civil-law framework no longer suffices. The debate no longer centers on the existence or availability of the asset and turns instead to the way this object is offered, governed and enjoyed in continuous consumer relationships.

This shift is decisive because certain digital assets already admit, in their very nature, multiple enjoyment and complex legal relationships, which weakens any entirely static understanding of the problem. Information need not be thought of on the basis <1>p. 577</1> of a rigid model of exclusivity, and the very idea of property can be read as a relationship conditioned by social function and by internal limits of legitimacy <2>Lacerda</2><3>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 50; p. 70)</3><4><5>644</5></4>. The IOC takes advantage of this opening, but shifts it to the field that matters. The question ceases to be only what exists legally and becomes how the enjoyment of this object is preserved, degraded, restored or made opaque to the consumer.

It is at this point that offer, quality, adequacy and trust come to operate in an especially important way. The CDC does not separate the offer from the product as if the former were an irrelevant promotional accessory and the latter an autonomous entity already closed in itself. Nonconformity with the offer and with advertising suffices to characterize consumer-law inadequacy, and quality defects by inadequacy are always measured in accordance with the consumer's legitimate expectation <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 252; p. 326-327])</2><3><4>645</4></3>. In IOCs, this means that the promised enjoyment cannot be reduced to the mere formal permanence of access. The immaterial object is also measured by the functional correspondence between promised utility and utility actually maintained in the course of the relationship.

The very breadth of the concept of product reinforces this reading. The CDC adopted a contemporary and broad vocabulary, directly linked to the results of production and circulation in the market, and not to the narrow category of the corporeal thing. The application of the consumer-law regime has always been explained by the placing of products and services on the market and by the consumption pole, not by a requirement of physical materiality of the supplied object (Nunes, 2018, [p. <1>p. 578</1> 89; p. 99])<2><3>646</3></2>. The interpretive tradition of the Code, therefore, already admitted incorporeal utilities and complex technological systems, including in contexts in which the acquirer's technical vulnerability justified legal protection <4>Filomeno</4><5>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 131; p. 267; p. 660])</5><6><7>647</7></6>. The IOC category merely makes this potentiality more precise for cases of governed enjoyment.

This precision also appears when one observes the link between immaterial product, trust and functional adequacy. Organized information can be understood as digital goods offered as products in the consumer market, and protection is anchored less in the static existence of the object than in the utility the consumer relies on and legitimately expects <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 78; p. 152])</2><3><4>648</4></3>. In products that depend on continuous services, the offer becomes the main criterion for measuring the legitimate expectation of use, and the duty to inform becomes decisive for assessing defect and adequacy <5>Miragem</5><6>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 87; p. 523])</6><7><8>649</8></7>. The IOC comes into focus precisely because it concretizes the immaterial product in a key oriented by the functional integrity of the promised enjoyment.

<1>p. 579</1> For this reason, the continuity of the bond and architectural opacity increase the weight of duties of predictability, reasoning and minimum verifiability. In a continuous consumption environment, protection applies not only to an isolated object, but to the conditions that make it consumable, because it is in them that the mechanisms of asymmetry and the points of possible relevant frustration are concentrated.

The IOC makes it possible to translate the phenomenon into manageable dogmatic language. It is not a matter of creating a “new CDC”, but of making explicit how the system already offers tools to control unilateral reconfigurations and practices of private governance when they impact adequacy, trust and restoration. It is precisely this reconstruction that will open space, in the following sections, for open auditability and functional value equivalence as <1>standards</1> for controlling administered mutability.

The methodological consequence of the item, then, is simple. The IOC does not replace the immaterial product of art. 3, paragraph 1. It concretizes it in a context of continuous and governed consumption. This prevents the object from being reduced to a technically granted and legally disposable permission, and also keeps the debate from being held captive by a static ontology of the digital asset. What the CDC protects here is not only the abstract existence of the object, but the acquired enjoyment in its functional, informational and relational integrity. This is the point that will later make it possible to deal with updating, modulation, downgrading and restoration without leaving the grammar of the system itself.

The incorporation of immaterial goods into the CDC's field of application is a possibility already inscribed in the legal framework of art. 3, paragraph 1, itself, whose wording consciously abandoned the narrower civil-law vocabulary of the “thing” to adopt the contemporary category of “product”, directly linked to the results of production and circulation in the consumer market. The CDC, following the contemporary concept, employs the term “product” and, in its definition, includes “any good”, designating it as “movable or immovable” and also “material or immaterial” <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 96])</2>. This doctrinal record is relevant because it shows that the recognition of immaterial objects of consumption does not represent a graft foreign to the system, but a coherent development of a possibility already expressly admitted by the law. The author himself observes that “product” already admits the categories “movable, immovable, material and immaterial” provided for in art. 3, §1 <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 160])</4>. <5>↩</5>

Nery Jr. <1>(2011, p. 544)</1> also observes that art. 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC allows the product to be read beyond corporeal materiality by conferring a legal regime of their own on products, defined as “any good, movable or immovable, material or immaterial”, which he considers a deliberately broader notion than that of “good” or “thing” in the Civil Code. The CDC does not make the configuration of the product conditional on physicality, and works with a category capable of encompassing incorporeal utilities placed on the consumer market. This openness takes concrete form, for example, in treating bank credit as an immaterial product subject to the elements of the consumer relationship <2>Jr.</2><3>(Nery Jr., 2011, p. 546)</3>. The CDC was not guided by the criteria of the Civil Code, but created its own system in which both materially consumable goods and legally consumable goods may form part of relationships subject to the Code <4>Jr.</4><5>(Nery Jr., 2011, p. 545)</5>. Reading the IOC as a concretization of the immaterial product makes dogmatically explicit a potentiality contained in the normative vocabulary of the system itself. <6>↩</6>

Just as what qualifies the object of consumer-law protection is not its corporeality, but its appropriable economic utility intended for the satisfaction of human needs, the doctrinal tradition understands the economic good on the basis of its aptitude to form part of relationships of circulation in the market, shifting the focus from tangibility to economic function <1>Filomeno</1><2>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 108-109])</2>. This openness is reflected in the recognition of immaterial utilities, such as bank credit, as legitimate products within the scope of the CDC <3>Filomeno</3><4>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 111-113])</4>. The reading of the IOC as a concretization of the immaterial product does not break with the classic ground of doctrine, it merely carries forward an openness that doctrine itself already recognized. <5>↩</5>

The identification of the contractual object of consumption within the scope of the CDC cannot remain tied to the traditional image of the isolated material good, as if legal protection applied only to a static thing detachable from its context of performance. In contemporary consumer relationships, what is offered to the consumer is a functional bundle of utilities, qualities, expectations and modes of performance that make up the very legal experience of the performance. Marques summarizes this shift by stating that, in the consumer contract, "what becomes important is the nexus of the performances and their balance (synalagma), not the performance itself, but its annexes, its quality, its functionality, the information that accompanies it, the status it ensures, the speed and the security of its rendering." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 180)</2>. The CDC system, supported by the theory of the social function of the contract, concentrates on the effect of the contract, so that the service rendered must be adequate for the purposes reasonably expected of it <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 183)</4>. This reinforces that the IOC can be understood as a contractual object of consumption precisely because its legal status emerges from the concrete way in which the performance is organized, made available, maintained and enjoyed. <5>↩</5>

The construction of the IOC as a concretization of the immaterial product provided for in art. 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC requires neither a rupture with the consumer-law grammar nor an artificial importation of categories foreign to the system. On the contrary, it stems from an evolutionary and functional reading of the microsystem itself, oriented by the need to understand contemporary forms of supply without abdicating the legal instruments already available for consumer protection. It is in this direction that Marques states that the adequate answer lies not in "proclaiming the uselessness of the traditional scientific instruments of law", but in the "use of the legal instruments we have, in particular the new Consumer Protection Code and the constitutional lines, so as to give reasonable and just answers to concrete cases" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 70-71)</2>. The contemporary consumer tends to become an accumulator also of services, doings and "immaterial goods" linked to well-being, security, leisure, status, information and credit, which requires the law to keep pace with this change <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 104)</4>. In this key, the IOC appears as an internal and coherent development of the system itself. <5>↩</5>

The recognition of the legal status of the digital asset constitutes an important starting point for the construction of the IOC, because it guards against relapses into a myopic dogmatics that would only grant legal density to the corporeal. Information, provided it carries appreciable utilities, may be treated as a legal good and, by meeting the conditions for the recognition of a new category of immaterial goods, blocks the denial of its relevance in a digital environment <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 52; p. 55; p. 71)</2>. This methodological continuity allows the thesis to maintain the legal recognition of the immaterial object while shifting the focus of the debate: instead of centering on the ownership or availability of the good, the problem turns to the way this object is offered, governed and enjoyed in continuous consumer relationships. The shift to the IOC does not deny the legal status of the digital asset, but reinscribes it in a key of its own linked to art. 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC, and becomes necessary when the debate reaches the functional integrity and the functional restoration of the consumed object. <3>↩</3>

The doctrine of digital assets itself offers elements that help shift the debate beyond the pure grammar of ownership by recognizing that certain goods admit multiple enjoyment. Information, as a good of plural enjoyment, makes it possible to overcome the classic view according to which a good could only be thought of on the basis of the exclusive enjoyment of a single subject <1>Lacerda</1><2>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 50)</2>. The same holds for the understanding of property as a complex legal relationship involving duties that condition the legitimacy of the exercise of the right, among them the social function <3>Lacerda</3><4>(Lacerda, 2024, p. 70)</4>. This inflection shows that the passage to the IOC does not depend on denying the doctrine of digital assets, but on carrying it to the point at which the pure language of ownership already proves insufficient. When the focus falls on how enjoyment is governed and altered in continuous consumer relationships, the IOC category is justified in order to shift the debate from the existence of the asset to the functional integrity of the consumed experience. <5>↩</5>

In the CDC, product, offer, quality and adequacy make up a single protective logic, which reinforces the dogmatic plausibility of treating the IOC as a concretization of the immaterial product. The Manual shows this when commenting on art. 18 and highlighting that the system recognizes not only defects that render the product unfit for consumption or diminish its value, but also defects arising from the disparity between its real characteristics and those conveyed in the offer and in advertising <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 326])</2>. The dogmatic consequence is decisive: the offer does not hover outside the product as an irrelevant promotional detail, but forms part of the very legal criterion for assessing its quality and adequacy. The Manual further observes that, in this third kind of defect, nonconformity with the offer suffices to characterize consumer-law inadequacy, even if there is no intrinsic defect in the good and no immediate material reduction of its value <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 326-327])</4>. Reinforcing this, quality defects by inadequacy are described as nonconformities relating to the performance of the product or service, to the fulfillment of its purpose and also to its durability, always “in accordance with the consumer's legitimate expectation” <5>Bessa</5><6>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 252])</6>. <7>↩</7>

The legal framework of the CDC proves broad enough to admit non-corporeal objects of consumption without any need for interpretive rupture. The application of the consumer-law regime is explained by the consumption pole and the placing of products and services on the market, and not by a requirement that the supplied object be physically material. The system regulates the products and services offered and sold on the market, a logic that holds both for corporeal goods and for supplied water and electricity or for money lent by a bank <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 89])</2>. Along the same lines, commenting on the legal enumeration of banking and financial services, Nunes notes that the express designation of these activities serves to prevent certain economic agents from escaping the scope of application of the CDC, and does not signal doubt about the immaterial nature of this type of service <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 99])</4>. This helps to show that the thesis does not inject a foreign body into the CDC; it merely develops a possibility contained in it. <5>↩</5>

The reading of the product in the CDC is not limited to corporeal goods, since the system itself recognizes that consumer relationships encompass movable and immovable, material and immaterial goods <1>Filomeno</1><2>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 267])</2>. The openness of art. 3 allows protection to apply to economically organized incorporeal utilities, as can be seen in the application of the Code to complex technological systems and software maintenance, in which the acquirer's technical vulnerability justifies legal protection <3>Filomeno</3><4>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 131; 660])</4>. Treating the IOC as a concretization of the immaterial product does not mean doing violence to the legal text, but making explicit a possibility already incorporated into the interpretive tradition of the consumer-law microsystem. <5>↩</5>

The reading of the IOC as a concretization of the immaterial product does not introduce a foreign body into the CDC, but makes explicit a normative potential already contained in art. 3, paragraph 1. Organized information can be understood as digital goods over which ownership and offer fall in the form of products that, under the terms of the CDC, may be immaterial goods <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 78])</2>. The importance of this breadth grows in the face of the economic growth of goods produced exclusively by means of computing, a scenario in which the legislator anticipated the regulation of the internet by making consumer protection norms fully applicable <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 152])</4>. The value of the approach lies in recognizing the functional breadth of the concept of product without imprisoning it in physical corporeality, allowing the CDC to treat techno-digital objects within a consumer relationship, shifting the focus from ownership to legally protected enjoyment. <5>↩</5>

By associating product, offer, trust and adequacy in a functional key, Miragem helps decisively to show that the IOC is not a foreign graft in the CDC, but an internal development of its protective logic. The author observes that, although distinct as to the specific duties imputed to the supplier, both liability for the accident and liability for the defect of the product or service are linked to the so-called theory of quality, which, in turn, is anchored in the protection of the consumer's trust. It is precisely this foundation that imposes on the supplier a general duty to offer products and services that are safe and adequate for the purposes intended for them <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 523])</2>. The notion of product in the CDC is not exhausted in the static identification of a good, but projects itself functionally onto the utility entrusted to and legitimately expected by the consumer. Miragem's reading becomes even more relevant when dealing with new products dependent on services provided by the supplier, continuous or not, under the assertion that, in these cases, the terms of the offer become the main criterion for gauging the consumer's legitimate expectations. According to the author, the fulfillment or non-fulfillment of the duty to provide correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information about the characteristics and qualities of the product is what will measure the consumer's legitimate expectation as to its use, including for purposes of contractual binding and of the supplier's liability under arts. 18 and 20 of the CDC <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 87])</4>. That is, the adequacy of the object is not read as an abstract quality enclosed in its materiality or in its nominal existence, but as a functional correspondence between the utility promised in the offer and the enjoyment actually delivered. It is precisely this perspective that makes the CDC speak of an immaterial product not only to open the doors of the system to incorporeal objects; but also so that its protection is organized on the basis of trust, offer, adequacy and restoration. Miragem thus helps to shift the debate from a civil-law ontology of the good to a functional reading of the object of consumption, in which what is relevant is not only the legal existence of the asset, but its aptitude to achieve, reliably and adequately, the purposes legitimately projected by the consumer. By concretizing the immaterial product of art. 3, paragraph 1, the IOC is consolidated through a consumer-law perspective oriented not by the mere ownership of the asset, but by the functional integrity of the promised enjoyment. <5>↩</5>
